To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the orthostatic tolerance of healthy HA dwellers, and of CMS patients is very good at altitude, and at sea level.

(i) the good orthostastic tolerance seen in high‐altitude dwellers at altitude, is also seen at lower altitude; and (ii) the orthostatic tolerance of chronic mountain sickness patients is not different from that of altitude dwellers without chronic mountain sickness.

orthostatic tolerance was similar in HA control subjects and CMS patients and was good at both altitude and sea level, and this was related to the fact that the CMS patients had impaired peripheral vascular responses and impaired cerebral autoregulatory responses, at least when examined at sea.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the physiological responses of the cardiovascular system to the stress of orthostatic stress and to the effects of altitude.
the effects of altitude on cardiovascular control and orthostatic tolerance.
the cardiovascular responses to orthostasis in subjects living at high altitude, and in particular with the responses of subjects with chronic mountain sickness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in high altitude dwellings, there is a high tolerance to orthostatc stress, which is not affected by chronic mountain sickness, but that this tolerance may not be related to the large blood volume, but to other factors, such as peripheral vascular and cerebvascular responses.
orthostatic tolerance, at least in healthy HA dwellers, is determined by a number of factors including plasma volume, peripheral vascular resistance and cerebral autoregulatory capacity.
orthostatic tolerance in HA dwellers is very good, and is not influenced by altitude.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the large blood volume seen in CMS is not the only factor that contributes to the good orthostasis in HA dwellers and CMS patients.
the large blood volume of high altitude dwellers is not an advantage for orthostatic tolerance.

the large packed cell and blood volume seen in HA dwellers and in CMS patients is associated with a good orthostatic response, which is maintained at sea level, but that there is an impairment in peripheral and cerebrovascular reactivity in CMS patients, which may contribute to the development of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the orthostatic tolerance of high altitude dwellers is not impaired at sea level.
orthostatic intolerance in CMS patients is not related to blood volume.

the large blood volumes in CMS patients are unlikely to be responsible for their good orthostatic responses, and that their responses are more likely to be related to the impairment of their cerebrovascular control.
